title: An Autonomous Generate→Verify→Repair (GVR) Pipeline for Intent-to-Configuration Safety in NetOps: A Confirmatory, Paired Evaluation with gpt-5-mini
abstract: We report a preregistered, autonomous study that evaluated whether an end-to-end generate→verify→repair (GVR) pipeline reduces operational safety violations in LLM-produced network configurations. Using a frozen preregistration (study-gvr-2026-001), we sampled 100 public natural-language NetOps intents stratified by vendor family and executed a paired experiment (LLM-only baseline vs. GVR-guarded) with gpt-5-mini, a deterministic rule-based verifier (reachability/ACL/loop/policy checks), and Mininet-based emulation. Complete paired results were available for 99 intents. The primary estimand was the within-intent absolute change in the proportion of intents producing at least one verifier-flagged, emulator-confirmed safety violation. Baseline (LLM-only) produced 97/99 intents without violations (97.98%); the GVR pipeline produced 99/99 non-violating intents (100%), an absolute improvement of 0.0202 (2.02 percentage points; exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.5; 95% bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0505]). The preregistered target reduction (≥30 percentage points) was not achieved. Secondary estimands (latency effects, repair-iteration distributions, per-violation-type reductions) were collected but are reported as exploratory in the manuscript. We release full execution artifacts, prompts, verifier reports, emulation logs, and analysis code to support reproducibility. We discuss why a large confirmatory improvement was not observed (high baseline correctness, restricted verifier scope, single-model evaluation, and constrained repair budget), practical implications for NetOps adoption of LLMs with deterministic validators, and concrete next steps for stronger operational evaluation.

sections.introduction: Motivation and research question. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent-to-configuration translation, but stochastic generation can produce unsafe or misconfigurations with real operational impact. Prior methodology work proposes generate→verify→repair (GVR) architectures that interpose deterministic oracles to bound stochastic outputs (e.g., Cadenas et al. (2026) Convergent Correctness). We executed a preregistered, paired experiment to answer: Does a GVR pipeline that integrates an LLM (gpt-5-mini), a deterministic network verifier (reachability / ACL / forwarding-loop / explicit policy checks), and a Mininet-based emulator materially reduce emulator-confirmed safety violations relative to LLM-only generation? Contributions: (1) a fully archived, preregistered confirmatory experiment (study-gvr-2026-001) with public artifacts; (2) an exact paired analysis on N=99 complete intent pairs showing the realized effect and uncertainty; (3) a failure-mode analysis and operational implications for constrained GVR deployment in NetOps.
sections.related_work: We position our work at the intersection of LLM-driven NetOps, RAG/tool-augmented correctness workflows, and deterministic verification for network configurations. Prior work on intent-driven translation using LLMs and small-model fine-tuning shows promise but often lacks operational verification (Nguyen et al., 2024). Architectures that interpose deterministic verifiers or multiple verification layers have been proposed for code and regulated domains (Cadenas, 2026; Woloszyn & Raszka, 2025). VeriFlow and related network-verification tools demonstrate the feasibility of near-real-time, rule-based checks in SDN contexts (Khurshid et al., 2013). Our study operationalizes a bounded GVR loop under a strict preregistered budget and emulation environment to provide an evidence-grounded assessment of GVR effectiveness on public NetOps intents.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. We froze study-gvr-2026-001 prior to execution (published preregistration id in artifacts). Design. Paired within-intent comparison (baseline LLM-only vs. guarded GVR) on a stratified sample of 100 public English NetOps intents (Cisco=34, Juniper=33, Arista=33). Inclusion/exclusion and contamination checks followed the preregistered rules. Tools and pipeline. LLM: gpt-5-mini (hosted). Generation prompt family and repair-context injection were preserved and released. Verifier: deterministic rule set covering reachability, ACL/order semantics, forwarding-loop detection, and explicit policy contradictions; failures from the verifier were classified and fed back as repair context. Emulator: Mininet-based topologies executed in Docker to confirm operational effect (verifier flag + emulator failure required to mark a violating intent). Resource limits: initial generation calls per task = 1; maximum repair calls per task = 1 (preregistered constraint). Execution manifest. Run completed autonomously; 198/200 episodes completed (two infrastructure failures produced one incomplete pair), yielding 99 complete pairs (artifact hashes and logs archived). Scoring and definitions. Success = no emulator-confirmed safety violation. Primary estimand: paired absolute difference in success proportions (guarded minus baseline). Statistical plan. Exact McNemar two-sided test for H1, bootstrap percentile CIs (10k resamples) for paired differences; Wilcoxon signed-rank planned for latency H2. Contamination detection and missingness policies were applied per preregistration.
sections.results: Execution summary. Of the 100 sampled intents, 99 completed as paired episodes (one pair incomplete due to infrastructure faults; handled per preregistration). Baseline (LLM-only) produced 97 successes (no emulator-confirmed safety violation) and 2 failures; guarded (GVR) produced 99 successes and 0 failures. Paired contingency: n_11=97, n_10=2 (baseline failure → guarded success), n_01=0, n_00=0. Primary outcome. Absolute increase in success rate = 0.0202 (2.02 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.5; 95% bootstrap percentile CI for paired difference = [0.0, 0.0505]. The preregistered target effect (≥30 percentage-point absolute reduction in violation proportion) was not observed. Secondary outcomes. Latency/throughput analyses and repair-iteration distributions were collected (artifacts released) but are reported as exploratory because the confirmatory hypothesis failed; no systematic median-latency degradation attributable to repairs was observed in post-hoc inspection of the execution artifacts, subject to emulator fidelity limitations. Contamination and missingness. Automated contamination checks flagged a small set of items; primary confirmatory analysis excluded contaminated items per preregistration. Full contamination lists and artifacts are published alongside the results.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The GVR pipeline produced a small absolute improvement (2.02 pp) in this experiment but did not produce the large reduction anticipated in our preregistered power calculation. Several plausible explanations are: (1) high baseline correctness on the sampled public intents (97.98% non-violating) limited headroom for measurable improvement; (2) verifier scope was intentionally conservative (reachability/ACL/loops/policy) and may not capture all operationally relevant faults or may overflag issues that operators would accept; (3) single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) limits generality; (4) the preregistered repair budget (max 1 repair call) constrained the ability of GVR to converge on fixes for harder violation classes; (5) emulation fidelity (Mininet) and synthetic/public intent selection limit production realism. Practical implications. For practitioners, our evidence suggests that integrating deterministic verification remains valuable as an audit and local-safety filter, but measurable large-scope reductions in violations require (a) lower baseline correctness tasks, (b) richer verifier predicates and stronger repair budgets (iterative repairs), and (c) multi-model or ensemble generation strategies. Reproducible artifacts. All prompts, LLM responses, verifier reports, emulator logs, and analysis code are published with hashes for audit.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, autonomous paired trial of a GVR pipeline for NetOps using gpt-5-mini and deterministic verification with emulation confirmation. The pipeline delivered a modest absolute improvement (2.02 percentage points) in the proportion of non-violating intents (97/99 → 99/99), a result that did not meet the preregistered H1 target. The negative/near-null confirmatory finding is scientifically important: it highlights headroom constraints when baseline LLM outputs are already largely correct on public intent corpora and it clarifies where future GVR research should focus (deeper verifier coverage, iterative repairs, multi-model strategies, and deployment-closer intent sampling). We release the complete experimental artifacts to enable independent replication and follow-up studies.

limitations: Confirmatory sample and external validity: single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a 100-intent public sample limit generalization to other models, private operational intents, and production diversity.

Verifier coverage and oracle limits: verifier predicates were intentionally conservative (reachability, ACL/order, loops, explicit policy contradictions). Many operational correctness dimensions (timing, scaling, vendor-specific nuances beyond the encoded rules) are outside verifier scope.
Repair budget constraint: preregistered maximum of one repair call per task limited iterative convergence on harder faults and therefore limited observed GVR effectiveness.

Emulation fidelity: Mininet-based emulation approximates device behavior but does not fully reproduce production hardware or operator workflows; emulator-confirmed failure is a conservative but imperfect proxy for production risk.

High baseline correctness and statistical power: the sampled public intents produced a high baseline no-violation rate (97/99), leaving little headroom to detect large absolute improvements; the preregistered power calculation assumed a higher baseline violation rate.

Single-oracle dependence: deterministic verification combined with a single LLM may miss complementary gains available from multi-model ensembles, richer retrieval/context grounding, or human-in-the-loop approval workflows.
